h: Glass, fire and a Roman emperor on the doorstep
p: Look out for the Great East Window, a vast medieval masterpiece telling the story of the beginning and end of the world, and the Five Sisters Window, with its tall, elegant grey-green glass. The Chapter House is another must, an octagonal room with no central column holding up its roof, and its stone carvings are full of cheeky faces and creatures if you look closely.

The Minster has come through some dramatic times. In 1984 a fire, thought to have been caused by lightning, tore through the roof of the south transept, and the heat cracked the famous Rose Window into thousands of pieces. It was painstakingly restored, and today you'd hardly know.
Outside the south door is a statue of the Roman emperor Constantine, who was proclaimed emperor in York in 306 AD. It's a reminder that the city's history goes way back before the Minster.
Allow a couple of hours, more if you're climbing the tower or exploring underground. Evensong is a lovely, free way to hear the choir, and services can affect access, so check before you go.

Then step out into the best of York. The Shambles, with its overhanging medieval buildings, is just round the corner, and you can walk a stretch of the city walls for great views back towards the Minster. Dean's Park, on the north side, is a peaceful green spot for a sit down, and the Treasurer's House is right behind the Minster.
